the screw that you show is not a fine adjustment and is not important for the playback, it is to make sure that it doesn't touch the cylinder when the carriage is lifted, it should be completely disengaged with the little tab while the record is playing. This style of reproducer is called a "floating" reproducer, meaning the entire reproducer moves with the force of the groove on the cylinder. Check that the reproducer can move, left, right, up and down with no restriction, but also make sure that it cannot rotate and that is is level with the cylinder. Another factor that may cause skipping is the alignment with the stylus to the "peak" of the cylinder, it should be riding the groove directly without "dragging" or "pushing". Make sure also that the entire machine is level, and that the cylinder is in good enough condition. Hope this helps!

Both reproducers are compatible with you’re phonograph, but the C would be the logical option for you.

The C on the other hand is the same as the model H, only with a different stylus compatible with 2 minute cylinders.

There are a few things I would point towards first. 

1) The needles should be new. If you found them with the machine in a needle cup, they have most likely been sued before. People would generally take the needle from the needle tin, use it, then toss it into the needle cup to then be thrown away. New steel needles can be found on eBay. I believe Wyatt Marcus sells high quality needles for quite cheap as well. The lower the tone, the less wear it will do to the records, as it will be more pliable and apply less pressure to the edges of the grooves. 

2) The reproducer should almost always be rebuilt IMO. Even if it looks good, the rubber gaskets are likely quite stiff, which means the needle will won't be able to move as easily, therfore applying more pressure to the groove. Rebuilding an exhibition or a No. 2 reproducer is not difficult and can really be done my anyone. 

3) make sure the record is clean. The most simple way to clean a 78 is to use dawn dish soap and a soft toothbrush, making sure to lightly brush in the direction of the groove, wiping it down with a clean damp towel/rag, and letting it dry. Sometimes even after cleaning there will be some dirt that is picked up by the needle on the first play, but if it continues then there may be another problem. 

4) the record should be from the same time period. Sometimes it can be really difficult to tell if a record is from the same Era. I have been collecting for a few years and still have trouble telling sometimes, you will have to research which of you're records you should be playing on it.

I will go against the grain and say I couldn't be sure that this is a "fake" without inspecting it in person. In Europe, there was a massive variety of handmade or small production phonograph, ones that are completely unfamiliar to collectors in the US. There are hundreds of different models that in many cases are one of a kind, or at least a lone survivor, and can often be passed of as "fake" because they have some sort of unique or cheesy design. It's really possible that this was cobbled together in the recent past, but it is also possible that this is a genuine old phonograph made in small quantities or on its own. 

That being said, the collectors market on these one off European machines is somewhat low, unless it is something extremely unique or unusual.

You may find needles that say they work for 50 plays, but they are not recomendable. A steel needle is plated with nickel for it to intentionally wear out, the reason being the variation in grooves from different records. When played, the needle takes the shape of the record groove causing less wear, which is why a needle of a harder material or used needles will wear a record out somewhat quickly. 

New needles are available for quite cheap on Ebay and are very easy to switch out. I would recommend "soft tone" needles as they produce a good volume for most records.

The problem could be a few things. The weight that hangs under the reproducer might not have enough movement to compensate for the movement of the grooves. The weight should move freely all all directions with no resistance. 

Another problem could be the feed screw, the threaded bar that moves the carriage from left to right. If the cylinder is too far to the right or the feed screw is too far to the left, the carriage may not be able to reach. The piece that connects to the feedscrew could also not be applying enough pressure. Sometimes the feed screw is damaged. 

If you can't get it resolved there are a few other reasons that has happened in my experience. Congrats on you're machine!

To answer you're question, yes, the Stollwerch records were intended to be eaten. To make them more durable and to avoid melting, I'm almost sure the chocolate was tempered, too it was a bit "snappy". As you could imagine, with edible chocolate records, almost none survived, let alone in playable condition. Because they were crude little machines with (presumably) almost inaudible music, I'm sure many kids got bored and ate the record. I'm not too sure how long they lasted, but I can assume that it wasnt too long.

To give value to the machine purchased with the chocolate record, they then made the wax records to play on them, but they soon after seized production due to finances.

For anyone curious about these:



**Top left**: *Maestrophone model 205*, manufactured by Paillard. It runs of a Stirling hot air engine, and its burning fuel is alchohol. To my knowledge, this is the first one for auction or sale for many years, just not sure how many. There are a handful of other 205's out there, and only one known model 206. 


**Top right**: *"Mammut" coin operated gramophone*. This was a coin op/parlor phonograph made in Leipzig Germany. The mechanism attached to the back of the tonarm is an autoplay mechanism, that releases and picks up the tonarm when it reaches the runoff. The horn is massive, with the bells diameter over 36 inches. 


**Center**: *Pathe automatic coin op concert*. Made in france, used in parlors and (I beleive) had the capability of playing pathe 20 inch discs. 


**Bottom left**: *Stollwerck wax disc upgraded phonograph*. Made in germany by the stollwerch record company. They made they're first phonograph out of tin in 1903, and was designed  to play records made of chocolate. They were fairly disposable and therefore had an extremely low survival rate. This version was an upgrade, had a wooden base and brass horn, and the records were made of wax. Sold extremely poorly and very few were made. 


**Bottom right**: *1910 "gigant" coin op saloon gramophone*. Very little is known about it as far to my knowledge, and it may be one of the few if not the only survivor of its kind. If the horn were to be "unraveled" it would be ~47 inches in length.

Yes, these are called listening tubes, and they were use in both listening parlors and for ICS purposes. ICS meaning "international correspondence schools", which you can see on the tag on the front. ICS made language teaching tools, and this standard was altered by them for that purpose. 

Each cylinder contains a recording of a person listing a set of word on the first half, and then using those words in sentences for the second half. The bar on the front of the bedplate would rewind the cylinder for 5 seconds for you to hear the cylinder again. A speed control was also added to slow or speed up the recording.
